text: Hadley had been awake since four, doing the arithmetic again on the back of an electricity bill. Rent due on the first. The card with the lowest limit was already at its ceiling, and the one with the kinder interest had been frozen after a single missed payment in March. Her son's orthodontist had sent a letter in red. In the next room Eli was asleep on the couch under his hoodie, his phone glowing on the floor where he had dropped it, and she did not want to wake him to ask about the job interview he had quietly stopped mentioning. She opened the bank app for the fourth time and watched the balance refuse to change. She had sold the good coat, the wedding china, and two evenings a week to a catering company that paid in cash and never on time. Nothing she did was enough, and the feeling was no longer sharp but total, like standing in water that kept rising. She wrote three emails to three landlords, deleted two, and sent the third with trembling fingers, begging for six more weeks. Then she sat at the table with her palms flat on the wood, desperate for one number to come out right, and it would not, and she was too tired to pretend otherwise.

Posting here because I don't know where else to go at 3am. I'm 41, separated, two kids under ten, and my ex has stopped paying her half of the childcare since she moved in with her new partner. I have no savings left after the lawyer retainer. My car got towed last week for the unpaid permit and the impound fee is 340 dollars I do not have. I've been picking up overnight shifts at the warehouse, which means I sleep in the afternoons and miss school pickups, and the school sent a letter about attendance. I just feel like I'm drowning in slow motion, and every time I bail water out another hole opens. I've applied for emergency assistance twice. One office lost my form and the other said I earn too much by about forty dollars a month. Forty dollars. I am desperate in a way I didn't know a person could be and still get up and make lunch. If anyone has been through a custody fight on no money, or knows a food bank that doesn't ask for paystubs, please tell me. I'll answer everything and I won't argue with anyone.

Dear Marcus, I'm writing because I can't say this on the phone without falling apart. The practice is going under. The landlord has given us until the end of the month, and the bank has stopped returning my calls. I have borrowed against my mother's house, which she does not know about, and I have told Lena we'll be fine. We won't be. I am desperate to find a buyer for the equipment before the auction, and I need you, specifically, because you still have the contacts from the Denver job. Anything you can do, however small, would help. I know we haven't spoken properly since the argument at Christmas, and I know I said things I can't take back. I'm not asking you to forgive me. I'm asking because there is no one else who knows what the place was like when it was good. Please call me tonight, whatever time. I'll be up. I've been up for nine days. Yours in more trouble than I can explain, Dan.

Day 31 of no word from the agency. Checked the inbox at 6:14, 7:02, 8:40. Nothing but the newsletter from the job board and a survey asking how I feel about my candidate experience. Ha. Sold the bike for 90 dollars to a guy who haggled me down from 120 and then said thanks like he'd done me a favor. Took it. The electric bill is due Friday. Rang the credit union, got a recording, rang again, got a human who said I'd need to come in person with three months of stubs. Walked there. Stood in line behind a man arguing about a parking ticket. Left the paperwork at the desk. Bought a bag of rice and a jar of peanut butter with the last twelve dollars and ate standing in the kitchen, the light off so I wouldn't see the stack of envelopes on the counter. Dana's text: call me when you can. I typed ok and deleted it four times. Set two alarms for tomorrow. Tried to sleep. Kept rehearsing the phone call to my mother where I say I'm fine. Her number sits at the top of the list, and my thumb keeps hovering over it.

The notice came taped to the door of Unit 4B, folded once so the red stamp faced outward. Teodora read it in the stairwell with her keys still in her hand. Forty-eight hours to vacate; the new owner wanted the place empty by Friday. Her daughter was at school across town, the bus pass had expired, and the shelter on Fulton Street had a waiting list the length of a city block. She stood there a long time. Then she went down the stairs and knocked on the super's door and asked, in her careful English, whether there was any chance of one more week. He looked at her shoes and then at the stroller folded against the wall, and said he would call someone. She thanked him twice. Upstairs she packed the kitchen first, because kitchens were heavy, then the bathroom, then the clothes she could not afford to replace. Her hands kept moving faster than her thoughts. Each box she taped shut felt like one more door closing in a house with no other exits. By dark the apartment echoed. She sat on the one chair left and pressed her palms against her eyes until she saw colors, and she prayed, not for a miracle, only for the phone to ring with something she could hold onto.
